title: 100 AI People to Watch in 2027: The Bets Behind Them
dek: The research, open infrastructure and business decisions behind AI’s next chapter. One documented contribution and one testable 2027 thesis for every person.

seo.title: 100 AI People to Watch in 2027 | Visionary Talks
seo.description: Meet 100 AI researchers, engineers and founders through their documented work, the businesses behind it and the milestones to watch in 2027.

limitations: Selected public-record research, not interviews or a comprehensive archive search.
Some entries use explicitly historical contribution records instead of asserting unconfirmed current employers.
Company financial statements are attributed, not audited by Visionary Talks.
No industry-representative demographic, influence or wealth ranking is inferred from this editorial selection.

people.name: Alexander Wei
people.hook: Reasoning needs an auditable result
people.fact: Wei identifies his OpenAI research role and lists his participation in the CICERO team.
people.analysis: The business question concerns the gap between an impressive answer and an argument that can survive external checking. Reliable reasoning could reduce expensive expert review, but the review burden is part of the product economics.
people.watch: Publish reasoning results with inspectable artifacts and clearly attributable contributions.
people.risk: A benchmark improvement that does not transfer to useful, verifiable work.

people.name: Jerry Tworek
people.hook: The people behind reinforcement learning
people.fact: OpenAI credits Jerry Tworek with overall leadership within its reasoning-research section.
people.analysis: That is a more precise starting point than a talent-market headline. I want to understand whether the training approaches associated with reasoning systems become repeatable tools for useful work.
people.watch: Document a subsequent system or research artifact and its reliability outside a curated demonstration.
people.risk: Treating a historical leadership credit as proof of current employment or sole authorship.

people.name: Jason Wei
people.hook: Making reasoning usable
people.fact: Wei says he works at Meta Superintelligence Labs and lists chain-of-thought and instruction-tuning work.
people.analysis: I am interested in the cost of turning a promising research technique into a dependable user experience. More reasoning is valuable only when the extra computation improves the result enough to justify its cost.
people.watch: Show reproducible improvements on tasks where quality and inference cost are both reported.
people.risk: A technique that improves a test score while making ordinary work slower or less dependable.

people.name: Hongyu Ren
people.hook: Attribution before the talent story
people.fact: Hongyu Ren appears among the foundational contributors to o1 reasoning research.
people.analysis: I would follow subsequent attributable research rather than use recruiting reports as a proxy for technical progress. The economic question is whether the work improves the cost or reliability of a reasoning system.
people.watch: Release a documented contribution that can be evaluated separately from employer prestige.
people.risk: Confusing participation in a large team with individual responsibility for every result.

people.name: Sholto Douglas
people.role: Research discussed in a first-person interview
people.hook: Where the reward signal comes from
people.fact: Sholto Douglas discusses reinforcement learning and the difficulty of specifying useful rewards outside games.
people.analysis: I am watching that design problem because businesses need agents rewarded for finishing the right task, not merely producing persuasive output. A cheap automated reward that misses the real objective can create expensive errors.
people.watch: Demonstrate generalization to new tasks with transparent success criteria.
people.risk: Reward hacking or narrow training success presented as broad competence.

people.name: Joshua (Josh) Batson
people.hook: A model’s explanation is not its mechanism
people.fact: The contribution section credits Joshua Batson with leading the overall circuits project and helping develop its methodology.
people.analysis: This is a useful documentary distinction: a model’s fluent explanation is not evidence of how it reached an answer. I am watching whether mechanistic analysis becomes practical enough to help diagnose failures before deployment.
people.watch: Show interventions that identify and reduce specific failure modes across more than one model.
people.risk: An attractive visualization that does not reliably predict behavior.
detail: The record is unusually helpful about individual responsibility. Its contribution section separates project leadership, graph computation, interventions and visualization. I would preserve that attribution rather than describe one researcher as the person who explained an entire model.

My commercial question is whether an explanation changes a decision. If a method identifies a failure but cannot predict when it will recur or help prevent it, its value remains narrower than a buyer might assume. The next step is a reproducible intervention, not a more elaborate diagram.

people.name: Julian Schrittwieser
people.role: Contributor describing the project’s published work
people.hook: Reasoning that a checker can inspect
people.fact: Schrittwieser describes the AlphaProof system and links its published mathematical-reasoning paper.
people.analysis: Formal checking offers a clearer success condition than a convincing paragraph. I am watching whether that discipline spreads to useful software or scientific reasoning, while keeping formal benchmarks separate from commercial readiness.
people.watch: Make more results and their checking procedure accessible to outside researchers.
people.risk: Success confined to problems already shaped for a formal system.

people.name: Neel Nanda
people.hook: Reverse-engineering the model
people.fact: Nanda says he leads DeepMind’s mechanistic interpretability team and identifies TransformerLens among his projects.
people.analysis: I see interpretability as an attempt to lower the cost of understanding failures that ordinary testing misses. The interesting business consequence would be better deployment decisions, rather than an explanation attached after something goes wrong.
people.watch: Produce reusable methods that help users locate actionable problems in deployed systems.
people.risk: Explanations that are informative to researchers but too fragile or costly for operational use.

people.name: Jack Parker-Holder
people.hook: Training environments without building every world
people.fact: Parker-Holder describes work on world models and points to Genie as an example.
people.analysis: Synthetic environments could change the economics of training agents, but a convincing generated scene is not automatically a faithful simulator. I am watching the link between simulated experience and measurable performance elsewhere.
people.watch: Show that agents trained in generated environments improve on independent real-world tasks.
people.risk: Visual plausibility mistaken for physical accuracy or reliable transfer.

people.name: Lilian Weng
people.hook: Separate self-improvement from the slogan
people.fact: Weng’s July 2026 notes discuss recursive self-improvement; her blog also examines test-time computation.
people.analysis: Her useful contribution is making the technical distinctions inspectable. I would separate better outputs, better training pipelines and a system modifying itself, because their evidence requirements and business implications are different.
people.watch: Explain a concrete feedback loop with measurable gains and its remaining constraints.
people.risk: A broad self-improvement claim with no clear baseline or independently checkable outcome.

people.name: Liam Fedus
people.hook: What a founding round needs to produce
people.fact: The investor names Liam Fedus as a co-founder and describes a $300M founding round dated September 30, 2025.
people.analysis: I would judge the scientific bet by reproducible experiments and the cost of obtaining useful results. Capital provides room to attempt the work; it does not establish that an AI scientist or a profitable laboratory already exists.
people.watch: Produce independently inspectable experimental results and explain the laboratory loop.
people.risk: Large financing without evidence of useful scientific throughput.
detail: The investor's round amount is documented; a company valuation is not stated in that opened record. I would resist filling the gap by treating a fundraising discussion as a completed financing. The dated capital ledger separates what was announced from what a secondary headline might imply.

The cost of scientific progress includes equipment, experiments, repeat attempts and expert interpretation. That makes the financial test different from a software demonstration: I want to know whether useful experimental throughput improves, and which parts of the loop still require people.

people.name: Misha Laskin
people.hook: Announcing a model and delivering it are different events
people.fact: The October 5 announcement promised the model’s weights and supporting artifacts later that month.
people.analysis: My focus is the sequence from announcement to accessible artifacts to independent evaluation. A model’s economic usefulness depends on the cost of serving useful outputs, not simply the size of its parameter count.
people.watch: Release usable artifacts and establish reproducible performance and serving costs.
people.risk: Company-only comparisons or limited access that prevents outside testing.

people.name: Luo Fuli
people.hook: Efficiency is also an engineering problem
people.fact: Fuli Luo appears on the report’s author list for a model using a mixture-of-experts and hybrid-attention architecture.
people.analysis: The question for 2027 is whether the serving system captures the architecture’s intended savings under actual workloads. A theoretical reduction is useful only if engineering turns it into reliable, cheaper service.
people.watch: Report deployment-level cost and latency alongside quality on comparable tasks.
people.risk: Architectural efficiency claimed without measuring the full serving pipeline.

people.name: Yao Shunyu (Vinces Yao)
people.hook: Learning from feedback without retraining every time
people.fact: Shunyu Yao is a co-author of research that uses linguistic feedback and episodic memory to improve an agent’s subsequent attempts.
people.analysis: That raises a practical question about where improvement should happen: in the model weights, the surrounding software or the task history. I would compare those choices by reliability, maintenance effort and cost.
people.watch: Demonstrate useful feedback loops on new tasks with safeguards against bad memories.
people.risk: An agent carrying forward a mistaken explanation as if it were verified experience.

people.name: Lin Junyang (Justin Lin)
people.hook: Open models need a usable deployment path
people.fact: Junyang Lin is listed among the authors of the Qwen2 model-family report.
people.analysis: The business question concerns the combination of model capability, accessible artifacts and practical deployment. The paper documents a research contribution; it does not establish subsequent financing or current employment.
people.watch: Produce accessible research or products with clear license terms and independently measurable usefulness.
people.risk: A changing employer or fundraising story substituting for evidence about the product.

people.name: Yang Zhilin
people.hook: Agentic models need workflow economics
people.fact: Zhilin Yang appears on the author list of the Kimi K2 report, which describes an agentic model and released checkpoints.
people.analysis: My focus is the cost of completing an entire workflow, including retries and tool use. A good benchmark result can be a starting point, but it does not establish a low cost per successfully completed business task.
people.watch: Provide reproducible task-level results with total serving and retry costs.
people.risk: A high headline score that masks expensive or unreliable execution.

people.name: Chelsea Finn
people.hook: The robot has to learn outside the demonstration
people.fact: Finn identifies her Stanford appointment, Physical Intelligence co-founding role and research on learning through robotic interaction.
people.analysis: The business question concerns the amount of new data and human intervention needed when a robot encounters an unfamiliar setting. That determines whether a general-purpose system can scale beyond a carefully prepared environment.
people.watch: Demonstrate useful transfer across tasks, objects and settings with intervention rates disclosed.
people.risk: A successful video that leaves setup labor and failures out of view.

people.name: Sherry Yang
people.role: Assistant professor and staff research scientist
people.hook: Generative models as environments for action
people.fact: Sherry Yang identifies her NYU and DeepMind roles and a focus on reinforcement learning and generative modeling.
people.analysis: I am interested in how models support decision-making, rather than just generate plausible outputs. The economic test is whether that research reduces the data or experimentation needed for a useful agent.
people.watch: Show improvements that transfer from generated or learned environments to independently evaluated tasks.
people.risk: A simulated result whose assumptions do not survive contact with the intended application.

people.name: Levent Alpöge
people.role: Researcher named in a contested priority account
people.hook: Credit and checking belong in the same story
people.fact: OpenAI’s September account discusses Alpöge’s work and acknowledges priority concerning a forced-Euler result.
people.analysis: I would keep that interested account separate from an independent resolution of the mathematics or credit dispute. AI-assisted research needs an inspectable chain of attribution as well as a checked result.
people.watch: Publish clear provenance, accessible arguments and independent scrutiny of the relevant claims.
people.risk: Treating one party’s account as a settled finding about either the mathematics or another researcher.

people.name: Sara Hooker
people.hook: The hardware can select the winning idea
people.fact: Sara Hooker examines how available hardware and software can favor particular research directions.
people.analysis: I find that framework useful when evaluating supposedly inevitable AI architectures. Technical success can reflect an ecosystem’s existing investments as well as the merits of the algorithm, which affects who can compete.
people.watch: Show practical alternatives that preserve useful quality while changing resource requirements.
people.risk: An efficiency claim that works only after shifting unreported costs elsewhere.

people.name: Joelle Pineau
people.hook: Research leadership meets enterprise constraints
people.fact: Cohere lists Joelle Pineau as Chief AI Officer and describes an enterprise-focused AI platform.
people.analysis: The question for 2027 is whether research becomes useful inside organizations with private data and operational constraints. The decisive evidence would be dependable deployment and repeatable customer value, rather than a new model alone.
people.watch: Document enterprise uses with clear evaluation, data-control boundaries and durable adoption.
people.risk: Product announcements without evidence of renewal or improved workflow outcomes.

people.name: Woosuk Kwon
people.hook: A business around an open inference engine
people.fact: Inferact names Woosuk Kwon among its founders and announces $150M raised at an $800M valuation on January 22, 2026.
people.analysis: What matters next is how commercial engineering support interacts with the open project. Sponsoring an engine is different from owning all of its software, community or downstream value.
people.watch: Demonstrate useful upstream improvements and dependable production service.
people.risk: Commercial adoption growing while community stewardship or portability weakens.

people.name: Ying Sheng
people.hook: Inference and training infrastructure share the bottleneck
people.fact: AMD’s event biography identifies Ying Sheng as RadixArk co-founder and CEO and an SGLang co-creator and core contributor.
people.analysis: I am watching the engineering that turns open models into reliable services. The company’s separate funding record names a co-led round; neither record makes SGLang a proprietary asset or proves performance claims.
people.watch: Report comparable throughput, latency and quality, with useful contributions flowing upstream.
people.risk: Comparisons that change hardware, batch size or quality targets between systems.
detail: The financing record is specific about roles too: Accel led and Spark Capital co-led. That is a small correction, but it illustrates why I trace the original announcement rather than summarize an aggregator. The disclosed post-money basis is also preserved in the table.

For the technical bet, I would compare the entire workload: hardware, batch sizes, latency targets, quality and utilization. A fast kernel is valuable, but a buyer pays for a service that must remain fast and dependable under changing traffic. Those are the outcomes I would track.

people.name: Georgi Gerganov
people.hook: Commercial backing without abandoning the community
people.fact: The February 20 announcement says Gerganov and the team are joining Hugging Face while retaining technical direction and community autonomy.
people.analysis: I see the governance terms as part of the business story. Support can make maintenance sustainable, but the value of local inference also depends on users continuing to control how and where their models run.
people.watch: Keep releases, contribution rules and technical decisions consistent with the stated autonomy.
people.risk: A change in sponsorship that gradually makes users dependent on a closed service.
detail: This is a counterexample to an overly simple claim that successful open-source projects become private companies. The announcement describes institutional support alongside a commitment to autonomous technical direction. That commitment is something readers can revisit through releases and governance, rather than accept as a permanent guarantee.

The economic question is who can continue to use the work and on what terms. Portability and local control can be valuable without producing a large personal-wealth estimate for a maintainer. I would follow maintenance, usable releases and community participation before assigning a commercial outcome.

people.name: Tri Dao
people.hook: Reducing memory traffic, not just buying more chips
people.fact: The repository credits Tri Dao and collaborators for FlashAttention and Dao for FlashAttention-2.
people.analysis: I am watching improvements that let existing hardware do more useful work. An optimization can change cost per task across many products, but the effect depends on workloads and integrations rather than a universal speed-up number.
people.watch: Reproduce gains on current hardware and real model workloads with quality held constant.
people.risk: A microbenchmark advantage that disappears in the complete application.
detail: The implementation links the named research to inspectable code. That is a stronger starting point than an unsourced statement that an optimization powers every major AI product. Its effect still depends on the model, hardware and surrounding pipeline.

I would report a gain against a stated baseline and keep quality constant. The relevant cost is completing a useful task, including memory movement, orchestration and other overhead. A component improvement can create broad value, but the paper's benchmark should not be silently converted into an application-wide saving.

people.name: Daniel Han
people.hook: Make adaptation cheaper to attempt
people.fact: The company record names Daniel Han as a founder and describes open-source reinforcement learning and fine-tuning tools.
people.analysis: The question for 2027 is whether more teams can adapt models without owning a large training organization. Lower setup cost matters, but the trained model still needs a reliable evaluation and a deployment budget.
people.watch: Show reproducible memory and cost savings with comparable model quality.
people.risk: Savings achieved by changing the task or accepting an undisclosed quality loss.

people.name: Omar Khattab
people.hook: Program the system, then measure it
people.fact: MIT lists Omar Khattab as an assistant professor in EECS.
people.analysis: His associated DSPy research direction puts attention on building and optimizing language-model programs. I am watching whether systematic evaluation can reduce the repeated prompt tweaking that makes agent projects costly to maintain.
people.watch: Demonstrate reproducible program improvements across new tasks and model changes.
people.risk: An optimized program that overfits its evaluation examples.

people.name: Lysandre Debut
people.hook: The model definition is part of the infrastructure
people.fact: Lysandre is among the announcement’s authors; the post describes interoperability across training, inference and deployment tools.
people.analysis: My focus is the maintenance work that lets a model reach users without every team rebuilding its implementation. Compatibility can be economically valuable even when it is less visible than a launch benchmark.
people.watch: Support new architectures promptly while improving predictable behavior across backends.
people.risk: Rapid integration that leaves incompatible defaults or poorly tested implementations.

people.name: Erik Bernhardsson
people.hook: Compute has to fit the developer’s workflow
people.fact: Bernhardsson identifies himself as Modal’s founder and CEO and describes earlier open-source work including Luigi and Annoy.
people.analysis: The business question concerns the gap between renting hardware and getting useful work done on it. A good compute platform reduces deployment and orchestration effort, but its value must survive comparison with direct cloud infrastructure.
people.watch: Document repeatable deployment savings and dependable service under changing workloads.
people.risk: Convenience that becomes expensive when usage grows or workloads become less predictable.

people.name: Lin Qiao
people.hook: A revenue run rate is not a profit figure
people.fact: The announcement identifies Lin Qiao and reports a $1.505B round plus an annualized revenue run rate exceeding $1B.
people.analysis: I would separate those measures before drawing a conclusion about the business. Serving revenue can grow alongside substantial compute costs; the useful question is what remains after delivering each workload.
people.watch: Provide clearer serving economics, customer durability and metric definitions.
people.risk: Revenue growth mistaken for high margins or cash generation.

people.name: Tuhin Srivastava
people.hook: Inference is a production engineering job
people.fact: Baseten identifies Tuhin Srivastava as CEO and co-founder and describes deployment engineering under real traffic.
people.analysis: The question for 2027 is whether the company can make reliability and latency predictable when models and customer workloads change. That is where infrastructure earns recurring revenue, rather than simply providing access to a GPU.
people.watch: Show sustained production performance with transparent cost and service boundaries.
people.risk: A tuned demonstration that cannot be repeated under customer traffic.

people.name: Gorkem Yurtseven
people.hook: Creative models need a distribution layer
people.fact: fal says Burkay Gur and Gorkem Yurtseven founded the company in 2021 to address AI infrastructure challenges.
people.analysis: The question for 2027 is whether a platform for generative media can make model access dependable enough for professional products. Distribution matters, but providers must distinguish their own contribution from the underlying models they serve.
people.watch: Demonstrate reliable delivery and useful developer economics across model changes.
people.risk: Model-provider dependence or volatile inference costs eroding the platform’s value.

people.name: Jeffrey Morgan
people.hook: Local deployment changes the control question
people.fact: The record names Jeffrey Morgan as a founder of a tool for running language models.
people.analysis: What matters next is how local model access changes privacy, portability and the cost of experimentation. Downloads and developer enthusiasm are useful signals, but neither establishes an enterprise business by itself.
people.watch: Make local deployment more dependable across hardware and model formats.
people.risk: Adoption figures that do not translate into supported, sustainable use.

people.name: Simon Hørup Eskildsen
people.hook: Search economics can shape the agent
people.fact: Eskildsen identifies turbopuffer as a search engine for object storage that he co-founded in 2023.
people.analysis: My focus is the cost of retaining and retrieving the context agents need. A cheaper search layer could change which products are feasible, but latency and correctness still matter when the data is large or frequently updated.
people.watch: Report useful search performance and cost across realistic data sizes and update patterns.
people.risk: Cheap storage offset by unpredictable retrieval or stale context.

people.name: Ankur Goyal
people.hook: Evaluation becomes an operating expense
people.fact: Goyal describes founding Braintrust after building evaluation tools at Impira and Figma; the February announcement states an $80M round.
people.analysis: The question for 2027 is whether evaluation becomes a repeatable part of deployment rather than a launch checklist. The business case is strongest when teams can connect a test result to a decision about reliability and cost.
people.watch: Demonstrate that monitoring detects consequential regressions and changes release decisions.
people.risk: A dashboard measuring convenient proxies instead of the failures customers experience.

people.name: Anastasios Angelopoulos
people.hook: Preference is useful, but it is a particular measure
people.fact: Angelopoulos identifies his Arena role and lists work on human-preference evaluation and conformal prediction.
people.analysis: What matters next is how evaluation platforms explain their populations, tasks and uncertainty. A preference ranking can guide a purchase, but it is not a universal measure of correctness or suitability for every workflow.
people.watch: Make ranking methods, sample limitations and task-specific results easier to inspect.
people.risk: A single leaderboard position treated as proof that a model is best for all users.

people.name: David Soria Parra
people.hook: Governance is infrastructure too
people.fact: The October 1, 2026 record lists David Soria Parra and Den Delimarsky as lead maintainers.
people.analysis: The business question concerns the rules that let tools connect to agents without every integration becoming a special case. The shared maintenance structure is more useful evidence than describing one person as the owner of an industry protocol.
people.watch: Demonstrate interoperable implementations with clear permissions and security boundaries.
people.risk: Broad support claimed despite incompatible behavior or unsafe authorization.

people.name: Gavin Uberti
people.hook: Specialization needs a durable workload
people.fact: Etched identifies Gavin Uberti as co-founder and CEO in its leadership section.
people.analysis: My focus is the trade-off behind specialized AI hardware: advantages can be large if the workload stays suitable, but chips take time and capital to develop. The full system, not an isolated operation, must justify the commitment.
people.watch: Show delivered systems with independently reproducible performance and operating costs.
people.risk: An architecture shift or integration constraint reducing the chip’s intended advantage.

people.name: Reiner Pope
people.hook: The compiler belongs in the chip story
people.fact: MatX names Reiner Pope as co-founder and CEO and describes work spanning silicon, compilers, kernels and models.
people.analysis: The question for 2027 is whether coordinated hardware and software design can improve useful training or serving economics. A company can be technically differentiated without the evidence yet establishing a production advantage.
people.watch: Deliver systems that outside users can evaluate on comparable end-to-end workloads.
people.risk: Impressive component results that do not become dependable customer performance.

people.name: Sharon Zhou
people.role: AI Chief of Staff, 2026 event listing
people.hook: Software determines whether alternative hardware is useful
people.fact: AMD’s event materials identify Sharon Zhou as AI Chief of Staff.
people.analysis: My focus is the practical software work around hardware choice. An alternative accelerator becomes useful when developers can run and maintain their workloads without rebuilding every part of the stack.
people.watch: Show smoother deployment, comparable quality and predictable support across important models.
people.risk: Hardware specifications improving faster than the software needed to use them.

people.name: Jerry Liu
people.hook: The document pipeline can be the product
people.fact: The May 2025 record identifies Jerry Liu and explains managed document parsing, ingestion and retrieval services.
people.analysis: The business question concerns the unglamorous preparation of enterprise data. An agent cannot use a document reliably if tables, structure or permissions are lost before the model sees it.
people.watch: Demonstrate accurate processing and useful retrieval on difficult customer documents.
people.risk: A polished answer that hides errors introduced earlier in the data pipeline.

people.name: Anton Osika
people.hook: Creating the app is only the beginning
people.fact: KTH identifies Anton Osika and Fabian Hedin as Lovable’s founders and describes natural-language app creation.
people.analysis: I am watching what happens after the first working prototype. A business application must remain understandable, secure and maintainable as users request changes. That continuing work determines whether creation becomes durable value.
people.watch: Show applications that remain useful through upgrades, maintenance and real customer traffic.
people.risk: Rapid creation followed by high repair costs or dependence on a fragile generated codebase.

people.name: Maor Shlomo
people.role: Founder associated with the acquired product
people.hook: A transaction headline is not personal proceeds
people.fact: Wix describes approximately $80M initial consideration, including employee retention payments, and conditional earn-outs through 2029.
people.analysis: For Maor Shlomo’s story, I would follow the operating product and the actual deal definitions. The consideration is not a verified measure of his wealth, and future conditional payments do not become cash already received.
people.watch: Demonstrate continued adoption and maintainable applications inside the larger company.
people.risk: Treating an acquisition announcement as proof of either personal wealth or future product success.
detail: The buyer's announcement describes a transaction with multiple elements. Approximately $25M of employee retention payments is included within the initial consideration, rather than simply added to it. Conditional earn-outs depend on later performance. Neither detail establishes Shlomo's own after-tax proceeds.

For the product, the next chapter is distribution and maintenance inside Wix. I would look for evidence of recurring use and successful application changes, rather than assume an acquisition ensures that every generated app becomes a durable business tool.

people.name: Mati Staniszewski
people.hook: Voice models become an enterprise service
people.fact: The update identifies Mati Staniszewski and reports that ElevenLabs surpassed $500M ARR in the first four months of 2026.
people.analysis: My focus is the shift from compelling generated voices to dependable communication workflows. ARR is a company-reported operating measure; the economics also depend on retention, inference costs and how customers use the service.
people.watch: Show durable enterprise usage with clear controls for consent, identity and quality.
people.risk: Rapid usage growth without dependable margins or trustworthy handling of voices.

people.name: Brendan Foody
people.hook: Human expertise stays in the training loop
people.fact: Mercor names Brendan Foody and Adarsh Hiremath as co-founders and co-CEOs and describes an expert network for training and evaluation.
people.analysis: The business question concerns the economics of human judgment as a model input. Labor-market participation, payment volume and company revenue are different measures; each needs its own definition before comparison.
people.watch: Demonstrate useful expert feedback and transparent outcomes for both customers and contributors.
people.risk: Volume claims that obscure quality, worker experience or the value of the resulting data.

people.name: Jesse Zhang
people.hook: A support agent must finish the customer’s problem
people.fact: Decagon identifies Jesse Zhang as co-founder and CEO and describes agents across customer-service channels.
people.analysis: I am watching resolution quality rather than how many conversations a bot handles. A low-cost answer can become expensive if it creates escalations, repeats mistakes or damages the customer relationship.
people.watch: Report resolution, escalation and customer outcomes with clear baselines.
people.risk: Containment rates that improve by making it harder for customers to reach a person.

people.name: Matan Grinberg
people.hook: Software autonomy needs an operating model
people.fact: Grinberg and Reyes announce a $200M financing at a $5B valuation on September 15, 2026, following the earlier Series C.
people.analysis: The business question concerns the cost of reviewing and maintaining agent-produced software. The later financing is a distinct company event, not a replacement date for the earlier round or a personal-wealth estimate.
people.watch: Show dependable software delivery with review effort, regressions and total task cost disclosed.
people.risk: Faster code production accompanied by a larger maintenance or security burden.

people.name: Mukund Jha
people.hook: Move from software creation to delegated work
people.fact: The April 2026 account names Mukund Jha and describes an agent operating through messaging interfaces.
people.analysis: The question for 2027 is whether familiar distribution channels make useful automation easier to adopt. Access to messages and tools creates operational responsibilities that a successful demo does not settle.
people.watch: Demonstrate reliable task completion with visible permissions, correction and human handoff.
people.risk: Convenient delegation without adequate control over mistakes or sensitive actions.

people.name: Cristóbal Valenzuela
people.hook: Creative output needs a production workflow
people.fact: The event materials identify Cristóbal Valenzuela as co-founder and co-CEO.
people.analysis: The business question concerns the transition from isolated generated clips to controllable creative production. Professionals need consistency, revision and usable rights, so the economically relevant output is a finished project rather than a striking sample.
people.watch: Show repeatable production workflows that creators can revise and deliver.
people.risk: High-quality samples that require too much manual correction to fit a real production budget.

people.name: Kareem Amin
people.hook: Employee liquidity is not growth capital
people.fact: The post by Kareem Amin describes employees being able to sell up to $55M of shares at a $5B valuation.
people.analysis: I would keep that employee-liquidity transaction separate from primary financing. For the product, I am watching whether automation improves useful commercial outcomes rather than simply increasing outbound activity.
people.watch: Demonstrate better conversion and accountable workflows using dependable customer data.
people.risk: A higher activity count with no improvement in business outcomes or data quality.

people.name: Jan Oberhauser
people.hook: Automation needs ownership and maintenance
people.fact: The press page identifies Jan Oberhauser as founder and CEO and dates the company’s founding to 2019.
people.analysis: What matters next is how teams connect models to established workflows. The value comes from dependable orchestration, permissions and exception handling; adding an agent to a flow does not remove those responsibilities.
people.watch: Show workflows that remain understandable and maintainable as tools and models change.
people.risk: Automation that saves time initially but becomes costly to debug or govern.

people.name: Robin Rombach
people.hook: Efficient visual generation still needs control
people.fact: The 2024 record identifies Rombach as a Black Forest Labs co-founder and describes work on latent diffusion and visual models.
people.analysis: What matters next is how efficient generation combines with controllable revisions. A professional user needs the intended result on demand, so the number of failed attempts belongs in the cost calculation.
people.watch: Demonstrate consistent editing and generation with clear licensing and reproducible quality.
people.risk: Attractive images that require excessive retries or cannot fit a customer’s rights requirements.

people.name: Alex Mashrabov
people.hook: A creative platform has to earn repeat use
people.fact: The conference record identifies Mashrabov as Higgsfield’s CEO and co-founder.
people.analysis: The question for 2027 is whether creators return for a complete workflow, not just to try a fashionable effect. The event’s financial language mixes run rate and ARR, so I have excluded it from the comparable operating table.
people.watch: Demonstrate durable creator adoption, usable revision tools and clearer metric definitions.
people.risk: Viral usage that does not become repeat demand at sustainable serving costs.

people.name: Grant Lee
people.hook: Capital efficiency needs the right denominator
people.fact: Lee reports $100M ARR, profitability, 50 employees and $23M initial funding, then separately announces a $68M Series B.
people.analysis: I would compare the milestones at their own dates. The later capital is not the amount used to reach the earlier operating milestone, and ARR is not recognized revenue. This is a useful claim to investigate, not an audited efficiency league table.
people.watch: Maintain useful customer retention while reporting more clearly on delivery costs and margins.
people.risk: A compelling company story whose definitions or period change between comparisons.
detail: The company's account places the operating milestone before the newly announced financing. Comparing $100M ARR with the later funding total would answer a different question from the company's stated milestone with $23M initial funding. The table retains both the event and its date.

I would also keep profitability as a company claim until the supporting definition and financial records are available. A lean headcount can be a useful fact about a business, but it is not a complete measure of efficiency when infrastructure, contractors and distribution costs differ.

people.name: James Cadwallader
people.hook: Being visible in AI answers is a business problem
people.fact: The record identifies James Cadwallader and announces a $180M Series D at a $1.8B valuation.
people.analysis: What matters next is how marketers distinguish an observed mention from a customer actually choosing the product. A measurement tool should connect its indicators to useful business outcomes, while acknowledging that model answers change.
people.watch: Demonstrate reproducible visibility measurements and evidence of commercially meaningful effects.
people.risk: Metrics improving without a credible link to discovery, purchase or customer value.

people.name: Noah Shinn
people.hook: An agent’s memory can help or mislead it
people.fact: Noah Shinn is the paper’s first listed author; the framework uses feedback stored as text rather than updating model weights.
people.analysis: The question for 2027 is whether that approach becomes a dependable ingredient in agent products. The research artifact establishes a contribution, rather than a later company-financing outcome.
people.watch: Show durable gains from feedback on independent tasks, with bad-memory handling disclosed.
people.risk: The agent reinforcing its own mistaken interpretation of an earlier failure.

people.name: Lourdes Agapito
people.hook: Research can become a production tool
people.fact: UCL attributes underpinning visual-synthesis research to Lourdes Agapito’s team and describes her co-founding role.
people.analysis: The business question concerns the practical conversion of research into a tool businesses can use repeatedly. The economic question is how much production effort is removed while preserving consent, identity control and a useful final result.
people.watch: Demonstrate dependable, authorized avatar workflows and measurable production savings.
people.risk: A lower creation cost accompanied by misleading identity use or unacceptable editing constraints.

people.name: Demi Guo
people.hook: The user needs to direct the result
people.fact: Pika identifies Demi Guo as CEO and co-founder in its team material.
people.analysis: What matters next is how consumer-friendly creation tools turn an idea into a controllable output. The useful measure includes revision effort and repeat use, rather than generation count alone.
people.watch: Give creators reliable ways to preserve intent and edit the result without starting over.
people.risk: Novelty-driven adoption that fades when users encounter production constraints.

people.name: Mikey Shulman
people.hook: The music business is part of the model business
people.fact: The September 2026 posts identify Mikey Shulman and describe model releases and music-industry partnerships.
people.analysis: What matters next is how creative control, permissions and distribution evolve together. A music model’s usefulness to customers depends on what they can do with its outputs, not only whether a generated song sounds persuasive.
people.watch: Explain usable rights and commercial terms while improving creator control and repeat demand.
people.risk: Rapid generation without a durable relationship with creators and rights holders.

people.name: Bar Winkler
people.hook: Integration is part of the product cost
people.fact: Wonderful identifies Bar Winkler and describes an enterprise platform supported by local deployment teams.
people.analysis: My focus is the economics of implementation. A model can be portable while the surrounding enterprise workflow remains highly specific; the labor needed to connect systems and manage exceptions affects margins and scalability.
people.watch: Demonstrate repeatable deployments and disclose where human engineering remains necessary.
people.risk: A services-heavy delivery process described as frictionless software scaling.

people.name: Chris Pedregal
people.role: Product founder associated with dated release notes
people.hook: Meeting context should survive the meeting
people.fact: Chris Pedregal appears as the author of releases including meeting chat, Windows support and shared team context.
people.analysis: The question for 2027 is whether a note-taking product becomes a dependable source of organizational memory. The value increases only if people can retrieve context accurately and manage what is recorded, retained and shared.
people.watch: Show useful retrieval and sharing with understandable recording and retention controls.
people.risk: Convenient summaries that quietly lose nuance or expose sensitive conversation context.

people.name: Zachary Lipton
people.hook: Clinical documentation has to be faithful
people.fact: Abridge identifies Lipton’s scientific and technology leadership and describes his work on robust machine learning.
people.analysis: What matters next is how documentation systems expose mistakes and support clinician review. Time savings are economically important, but I would not infer a clinical benefit from a product’s adoption or fundraising alone.
people.watch: Report accuracy, correction workload and operational effects with clear evaluation methods.
people.risk: Less visible documentation effort accompanied by consequential transcription or summarization errors.

people.name: Nikhil Buduma
people.hook: The workflow extends beyond the transcript
people.fact: The company announces Nikhil Buduma’s move from chief scientist to CEO and describes documentation, coding and clinical workflows.
people.analysis: The question for 2027 is whether broader integration produces useful operational outcomes without weakening oversight. A company's deployment statement is evidence of its approach, not independent proof of improved patient outcomes.
people.watch: Demonstrate measured workflow benefits and transparent handling of errors and corrections.
people.risk: Commercial expansion outpacing independent evidence of reliability.

people.name: Zachary Ziegler
people.hook: A cited answer still needs source discipline
people.fact: Sequoia associates Zachary Ziegler with OpenEvidence and links its clinical-information product.
people.analysis: The question for 2027 is whether information retrieval can remain useful while making the basis of an answer inspectable. Citations are an entry point for checking; they do not by themselves establish that the answer accurately represents the evidence.
people.watch: Demonstrate source-faithful answers, transparent updates and clear limitations.
people.risk: Authority implied by a citation that does not actually support the response.

people.name: Suchi Saria
people.hook: Useful alerts must fit the care team
people.fact: The company identifies Suchi Saria as its founder and describes real-time clinical signals drawn from patient data.
people.analysis: The business question concerns the relationship between a predictive model and the people expected to act on it. An alert’s business and clinical value depend on workflow, false alarms and the intervention it enables.
people.watch: Produce independent evaluations of useful interventions and their operational burden.
people.risk: A strong prediction metric that does not lead to reliable action in practice.

people.name: Joshua Meier
people.hook: A designed molecule must pass an experiment
people.fact: Index identifies Joshua Meier among Chai’s co-founders and describes a molecular-design business.
people.analysis: What matters next is how computational proposals become experimentally useful candidates. A partner announcement or prediction result does not establish a successful medicine; laboratory and development evidence must carry the next stage of the story.
people.watch: Publish reproducible experimental results and clarify what customers can use today.
people.risk: Technical promise mistaken for a validated therapeutic or a proven development shortcut.

people.name: Brian Hie
people.hook: Biological prediction needs experimental grounding
people.fact: Arc identifies Brian Hie as a co-senior author and describes releasing model code, data and weights.
people.analysis: I am watching whether open biological models help outside researchers ask better experimental questions. The immediate evidence is a research resource, not proof of a clinical product or a reliable simulation of every organism.
people.watch: Enable independent reuse with experimentally validated applications and clear safety boundaries.
people.risk: Prediction quality presented as proof that a designed biological system will behave as intended.
detail: The useful documentary finding is the set of released artifacts. Arc describes sharing data, code and weights, giving outside researchers a way to investigate the work. Access is a practical research advantage, but it does not guarantee that a proposed biological design will work.

My next test is external reuse tied to experimental evidence. A model can become a valuable foundation for research while remaining far from a clinical product. I would keep prediction, laboratory validation and therapeutic development as different stages, each with its own evidence.

people.name: Max Jaderberg
people.hook: Research leadership takes on a delivery obligation
people.fact: The November 2025 record appoints Max Jaderberg President effective January 1, 2026, after serving as Chief AI Officer.
people.analysis: I am watching the transition from model development to a company delivering drug-design work. The milestone that matters is external validation of useful candidates and workflows, with development stages kept distinct.
people.watch: Document experimental or clinical-development milestones with their actual stage and limitations.
people.risk: A partnership or candidate announcement treated as a proven medicine or realized revenue.
detail: The appointment has a clear effective date. That lets the article distinguish the announcement in November from the leadership change in January. Dates matter for operating milestones too: a planned study, a candidate entering development and a successful result are separate events.

I would follow the company through those events instead of infer progress from capital raised. Drug-design research can have substantial option value while its eventual commercial outcome remains uncertain. The watchlist should make the next evidence threshold easy to identify.

people.name: Emma Lundberg
people.role: Associate professor and Cell Atlas director
people.hook: The dataset can be the scientific advantage
people.fact: Stanford describes Lundberg’s work on spatial protein organization, cell mapping and virtual-cell models.
people.analysis: I am watching the quality of the measurements behind biological AI. Better models cannot compensate indefinitely for poorly characterized data, and a useful virtual cell must explain which behaviors it captures and which it does not.
people.watch: Connect model predictions to new measurements and reproducible cellular experiments.
people.risk: A convincing simulation whose assumptions are not validated outside its training data.
detail: A virtual-cell narrative can obscure the measurements that make a model useful. Lundberg's institutional profile identifies work on where proteins are located and how that relates to cellular function. The spatial information is part of the scientific question, not a decorative label attached to a general model.

I would look for predictions that lead to new measurements and survive experimental scrutiny. The model should state its scope: a useful representation of selected processes does not become a complete simulation of a living cell merely because the interface is persuasive.

people.name: Karol Hausman
people.hook: General-purpose robotics needs repeatable transfer
people.fact: Hausman identifies himself as a Physical Intelligence co-founder and lists work on robot learning and general-purpose skills.
people.analysis: What matters next is how much new engineering a robot needs for each deployment. Shared models could improve scalability, but the practical test includes intervention, setup and maintenance rather than a curated task video.
people.watch: Show reliable transfer across settings and disclose the human effort required.
people.risk: A general-purpose label applied to a system that needs extensive custom deployment work.

people.name: Deepak Pathak
people.hook: Learning from the world rather than a perfect dataset
people.fact: Pathak describes agents learning from raw sensory data and research spanning vision, learning and robotics.
people.analysis: The question for 2027 is whether those methods reduce dependence on expensive curated demonstrations. A robot that learns more economically still has to do useful work safely and reliably in the intended setting.
people.watch: Demonstrate new skills with lower data or supervision requirements and transparent failure rates.
people.risk: Training efficiency that comes at the cost of unpredictable behavior during deployment.

people.name: Bernt Øivind Børnich
people.hook: A household robot is a service commitment
people.fact: The October 2025 company release identifies Bernt Børnich and presents NEO as a home-robot product.
people.analysis: I am watching what a customer can actually rely on after delivery. Hardware reliability, human assistance, privacy and maintenance all belong in the cost of providing a useful household robot.
people.watch: Show real deployments with assistance requirements, uptime and service terms explained.
people.risk: An appealing launch that obscures intervention or support needed in ordinary homes.

people.name: Carolina Parada
people.hook: Embodied reasoning needs an action test
people.fact: The March 2025 post by Carolina Parada introduces vision-language-action and embodied-reasoning models.
people.analysis: What matters next is how language and visual understanding become dependable physical actions. The relevant evidence includes task success, adaptation and safety under changed conditions, rather than language fluency alone.
people.watch: Demonstrate robust task execution across hardware and unfamiliar environments.
people.risk: Reasoning that sounds plausible but fails when the action has physical consequences.

people.name: Max Junestrand
people.hook: Legal work needs traceable context
people.fact: Legora identifies Max Junestrand as CEO and co-founder and describes a platform for legal work.
people.analysis: The question for 2027 is whether legal teams can inspect and revise the steps between source material and final output. Time savings matter only alongside source fidelity, confidentiality and the professional review still required.
people.watch: Demonstrate repeatable workflow benefits with source tracing and appropriate human review.
people.risk: Fast drafting that transfers hidden checking costs to the lawyer.

people.name: Gabriel Pereyra
people.hook: Distribution and trust are part of the product
people.fact: The March 2024 record identifies Gabriel Pereyra and describes deployment and distribution through Azure.
people.analysis: What matters next is how a specialized AI product becomes purchasable and usable within a large organization. Distribution can accelerate adoption, but the product still has to justify its place in a professional workflow.
people.watch: Demonstrate dependable use with clear security, source verification and customer outcomes.
people.risk: Distribution reach mistaken for evidence of sustained customer value.

people.name: George Sivulka
people.hook: Research is only one stage of the financial workflow
people.fact: The June 2025 post identifies Sivulka and describes adding slide creation to retrieval and analysis workflows.
people.analysis: My focus is the handoff from evidence to a deliverable. A financial team needs a defensible chain from source documents to analysis to presentation, and errors can enter at every stage.
people.watch: Show accurate source-to-deliverable workflows with usable review and correction.
people.risk: A polished deck that makes unsupported conclusions harder to notice.

people.name: Gabriel Stengel
people.hook: The banking workflow is the unit of value
people.fact: Gabe Stengel authors Rogo’s April 29, 2026 announcement of a $160M Series D.
people.analysis: The question for 2027 is whether financial-workflow automation reduces total review and execution effort. A company’s financing is a dated capital event; it does not establish the accuracy of its analysis or the productivity of its users.
people.watch: Demonstrate accountable workflow outcomes with inspectable sources and review effort.
people.risk: Output speed improving while verification and correction costs rise.

people.name: Antoine Bordes
people.hook: Grounding intelligence in structured facts
people.fact: The January 2026 release identifies Bordes and describes his co-authored research on structured knowledge embeddings.
people.analysis: What matters next is how research translates into reliable systems under demanding operational conditions. Academic recognition establishes a contribution; deployment claims need separate evidence about testing, constraints and oversight.
people.watch: Explain validated performance and control boundaries in the intended use.
people.risk: Research pedigree used as a substitute for operational validation.

people.name: Oege de Moor
people.role: Founder associated with the company’s security research
people.hook: Count validated findings, not just generated exploits
people.fact: The June 2025 post says automated findings were reviewed by its security team before submission under platform rules.
people.analysis: For Oege de Moor’s story, that human-review step is economically important. I am watching how useful discovery, false positives and responsible reporting combine, rather than treating a leaderboard headline as fully unattended operation.
people.watch: Show independently acknowledged findings and transparent review and authorization practices.
people.risk: Large discovery counts that conceal duplication, rejected reports or substantial hidden labor.

people.name: Ekin Dogus Cubuk
people.hook: Materials research needs a physical feedback loop
people.fact: The company describes its founding team and a plan to combine AI with autonomous physical laboratories.
people.analysis: For Ekin Dogus Cubuk, I am watching whether the loop produces reproducible materials results. The company’s financing is recorded once alongside Fedus; a shared company event does not become two independent pieces of funding evidence.
people.watch: Connect proposed discoveries to inspectable experiments and useful properties.
people.risk: A prediction treated as a discovered, usable material before experimental confirmation.

people.name: Jonathan Godwin
people.hook: A named industrial deployment is a concrete lead
people.fact: The August 2026 post names Jonathan Godwin and describes licensing its CurieOS materials platform to BASF ECMS.
people.analysis: I would follow that relationship into evidence of actual industrial use. A named agreement is more specific than a general market claim, but it does not disclose realized revenue or independent proof of improved research productivity.
people.watch: Report attributable deployment outcomes and the stage of commercial use.
people.risk: An announced agreement remaining a pilot without measurable industrial value.

people.name: Kristen DiCerbo
people.hook: Start with the learning problem
people.fact: The organization identifies DiCerbo and describes her advice to begin technology decisions with the problem being solved.
people.analysis: The question for 2027 is whether AI tools improve learning outcomes rather than simply usage. Education requires a clear account of the teacher’s role, the student’s needs and what the evaluation actually measures.
people.watch: Demonstrate meaningful learning effects with appropriate comparisons and transparent limitations.
people.risk: Engagement or generated answers mistaken for improved understanding.

people.name: Alex Kendall
people.hook: Driving intelligence needs evidence on the road
people.fact: Kendall identifies his Wayve role and lists work on embodied AI, uncertainty and autonomous-driving models.
people.analysis: The business question concerns the progression from research to dependable deployment. The economics depend on the operating conditions, supervision and service required, which cannot be established by a capable-looking driving clip.
people.watch: Publish meaningful deployment and safety evidence with a clear operating scope.
people.risk: Expansion claims that omit constraints, intervention or the cost of supervision.

people.name: Beth Barnes
people.hook: Capability and useful productivity are different measures
people.fact: METR names Beth Barnes as founder and CEO and describes independent evaluation, productivity research and its funding arrangements.
people.analysis: I am watching evidence that can change a deployment or investment decision. The organization's time-horizon work measures a particular task distribution; its old chart page explicitly no longer updates, so I do not extrapolate it into 2027.
people.watch: Publish reproducible evaluations with limits, uncertainty and funding relationships clear.
people.risk: A benchmark result becoming a universal forecast of job automation.
detail: The organization discloses both funding and access relationships. Its about page says it has not accepted AI-company funding, while acknowledging tokens and access supplied by model developers. Those are different kinds of support, and readers deserve to see the distinction.

I would separate capability evaluations from studies of useful productivity. The historical time-horizon metric uses human-expert task duration in a specified suite, not the time a model can remain at work unattended. Its old page says it no longer updates; a forecast needs a current dataset and clearly stated assumptions.

people.name: Marius Hobbhahn
people.hook: An evaluator needs more than a dramatic example
people.fact: Apollo identifies Marius Hobbhahn as CEO and co-founder and describes research on AI scheming.
people.analysis: The business question concerns the path from a concerning behavior in an experiment to a useful evaluation or safeguard. The business relevance depends on repeatability, realistic conditions and a clear account of what the test detects.
people.watch: Demonstrate actionable evaluations and interventions with reproducible methods.
people.risk: A striking result whose setup does not represent the deployment being assessed.

people.name: Buck Shlegeris
people.hook: Design for a model that may not cooperate
people.fact: Redwood identifies Buck Shlegeris as Chief Executive Officer of the AI safety and security research nonprofit.
people.analysis: I am watching control methods that test whether oversight can remain useful even when a system behaves unexpectedly. The practical question is what they detect, what they miss and how much capability they sacrifice.
people.watch: Publish control evaluations with adversarial testing and clearly stated assumptions.
people.risk: A safeguard that works only when the monitored model is already cooperative.

people.name: Owain Evans
people.hook: A narrow change can have a broader consequence
people.fact: The nonprofit identifies Owain Evans as team lead and lists research on deception, hidden reasoning and emergent misalignment.
people.analysis: The question for 2027 is whether training changes produce unintended behavior beyond the targeted task. That matters to buyers who adapt a model for a narrow use and assume the rest of its behavior remains unchanged.
people.watch: Show reproducible results and practical ways to detect or limit unwanted generalization.
people.risk: Overgeneralizing from an experiment without identifying the conditions that produced it.

people.name: Dean W. Ball
people.role: Head of Strategic Futures, announced July 2026
people.hook: Policy work changes commercial constraints
people.fact: FAI says Ball joins OpenAI as Head of Strategic Futures on July 6 while retaining a non-resident fellowship.
people.analysis: I am watching where policy arguments become concrete operating rules. His move also changes the institutional perspective behind those arguments, which readers should distinguish from independent academic or public-interest analysis.
people.watch: Connect proposals to actual policy developments and explain institutional incentives.
people.risk: An advocacy position treated as a neutral forecast or settled rule.

people.name: Lennart Heim
people.hook: A threshold is an initial filter, not the whole risk assessment
people.fact: The authors argue that training compute can identify models for scrutiny but should not determine mitigations by itself.
people.analysis: What matters next is how resource-based policy adapts when algorithms and inference change. A measurable input can be useful while remaining an imperfect proxy for capability or harm.
people.watch: Explain how thresholds are complemented by model evaluation and revised as technology changes.
people.risk: A convenient numerical cutoff treated as a complete assessment of risk.

people.name: Kai Zenner
people.hook: Implementation can matter more than the headline law
people.fact: OECD describes Zenner’s digital-policy work for MEP Axel Voss and links his work on foundation-model regulation.
people.analysis: What matters next is how technical distinctions enter implementation and oversight. Companies need to know what actually applies to their systems; a historical biography’s negotiation language should not be mistaken for the current legal timetable.
people.watch: Clarify practical obligations through current official records and technical guidance.
people.risk: Commentary about proposed rules presented as the law currently in force.

people.name: Helen Toner
people.hook: Policy research needs a documented chain of reasoning
people.fact: CSET identifies Toner as Executive Director.
people.analysis: I am watching evidence about AI competition and governance that can survive inspection beyond its headline. The value lies in transparent sources and distinctions, especially where technical and geopolitical claims interact.
people.watch: Publish research with inspectable data and conclusions that remain within its scope.
people.risk: A broad geopolitical conclusion built from anecdotes or an unrepresentative sample.

people.name: Sarah Guo
people.hook: The investment thesis should survive the market cycle
people.fact: Guo describes an AI-focused venture firm built around companies using foundation models.
people.analysis: I am watching which investments produce durable businesses rather than brief distribution advantages. A fund’s commitments are managed capital, not the investor’s personal wealth or proof of returns.
people.watch: Explain how portfolio businesses retain value when underlying models improve or become cheaper.
people.risk: An investment narrative that depends on scarcity the market subsequently removes.

people.name: Nathan Benaich
people.hook: Make predictions inspectable, then score them
people.fact: Benaich describes annual predictions and returning to assess them in the State of AI report.
people.analysis: I am watching that accountability as much as the predictions themselves. An investor’s research can be useful while reflecting an investment perspective; readers should be able to distinguish evidence, selection and the author’s bets.
people.watch: Keep forecasts specific enough to evaluate and publish the outcome of earlier calls.
people.risk: Retrospective success claims that quietly change the original prediction.

people.name: Leigh Marie Braswell
people.hook: Product experience meets capital allocation
people.fact: The firm identifies Braswell as a partner and describes earlier engineering and product work at Scale AI.
people.analysis: What matters next is how that experience shapes judgments about infrastructure and applications. A named investment or board seat establishes a relationship, but it does not establish the investor’s personal stake or a realized return.
people.watch: Show businesses with durable customer value and explain the technical assumptions behind the bets.
people.risk: Portfolio valuation growth mistaken for demonstrated business durability.

people.name: Grace Isford
people.hook: The physical-world bet has a different delivery schedule
people.fact: Lux identifies Isford as a partner investing across software, computation and the physical world.
people.analysis: The question for 2027 is whether investment horizons match the work needed to deliver hardware, robotics or biology. Those businesses can have different validation and capital requirements from a software product, even when all use AI.
people.watch: Tie company milestones to their actual development stage and capital needs.
people.risk: Software-style growth expectations imposed on slower physical validation.

people.name: Simon Willison
people.hook: Test the tool before accepting the claim
people.fact: Willison identifies his open-source development work, Datasette and Django, and discloses sponsorship and product-preview relationships.
people.analysis: I am watching his practical approach to checking AI tools because buyers need reproducible examples and visible failure cases. Commercial access can inform useful testing while still requiring clear disclosure of the relationship.
people.watch: Publish examples readers can reproduce, including constraints and unsuccessful cases.
people.risk: A product impression presented as an independent performance study.
detail: His biography includes sponsorship and preview-access disclosures alongside the work itself. That is useful context for assessing a product test. A person can report valuable observations while having early access; the relationship should be visible rather than collapsed into a blanket independence claim.

The practical standard I would use is reproduction. Can a reader run the example, see the failure mode and identify the setup that produced it? That form of technical literacy can lower costly mistakes for businesses adopting tools faster than they understand their constraints.

people.name: Nathan Lambert
people.role: Researcher and author; departed Ai2 in 2026
people.hook: Open weights are not an open training recipe
people.fact: Lambert describes his work on Tülu and open post-training and says he is developing a new project after leaving Ai2.
people.analysis: The business question concerns the information needed to reproduce how a model was improved. A released checkpoint is useful, but it does not reveal every ingredient in the training process. The departure account does not name the new organization, so I would not infer a current employer from it.
people.watch: Release inspectable training recipes and evaluations that other teams can reproduce.
people.risk: An open label applied to artifacts that leave the important training choices inaccessible.

people.name: Dwarkesh Patel
people.hook: Interviews are evidence of what someone says
people.fact: Patel identifies himself as the podcast’s host and describes a format built around researched interviews.
people.analysis: My focus is the questions that expose assumptions about cost, capability and strategy. A first-person interview can establish a speaker’s view; it does not independently verify every forecast or private-company number stated in it.
people.watch: Press for specific mechanisms and revisit predictions against subsequent records.
people.risk: A persuasive interview becoming a substitute for independently checked evidence.

people.name: Shawn "swyx" Wang
people.hook: The people applying models need a shared vocabulary
people.fact: The organization identifies Shawn Wang and dates his AI Engineer essay and the first summit to 2023.
people.analysis: What matters next is how a professional community turns fast-moving tools into repeatable practice. Conferences and newsletters can accelerate learning, but attendance or audience size does not establish engineering quality.
people.watch: Make useful implementation knowledge accessible, testable and distinct from sponsorship.
people.risk: A growing community that amplifies fashionable claims faster than it evaluates them.

people.name: Sebastian Raschka
people.hook: Implementation exposes what a diagram leaves out
people.fact: Raschka describes reading papers and reference implementations, then building smaller versions to understand their details.
people.analysis: I am watching that bridge between research and working code. It can help readers judge architecture and evaluation choices for themselves, rather than rely on a summary that hides important assumptions.
people.watch: Produce reproducible implementations with clearly explained limits and evaluation choices.
people.risk: A teaching example mistaken for a production-ready system or a full reproduction of a frontier result.
